paragraphs.heading: The drowned edge of a continent
paragraphs.text: A continental shelf is the part of a continent that lies under fairly shallow sea, and the water above it is called a shelf sea. Although it is usually grouped with the ocean floor, it belongs not to the deep ocean basin but to the continent, as its flooded edge. A shelf around an island is called an insular shelf. Much of today's shelf area was laid bare when sea level fell during glacial periods.

paragraphs.heading: How big shelves are
paragraphs.text: Shelves cover about 27 million km², roughly 7% of the oceans' surface area. They average about 80 km wide, but some coasts have almost none, such as off Chile or western Sumatra, where an oceanic plate dives beneath continental crust. The widest, the Siberian Shelf in the Arctic Ocean, reaches 1,500 kilometers across. The water on a shelf is generally less than 100 m deep, and the seabed tilts only about 0.5°, with less than 20 m of vertical relief.

paragraphs.heading: The shelf break
paragraphs.text: The shelf usually ends where the seabed starts to steepen, a point called the shelf break. With a few exceptions, the break sits at a strikingly even depth of about 140 m, probably a mark of past ice ages when the sea stood lower. Below it is the continental slope, averaging 3° but ranging from 1° to 10°, and often cut by submarine canyons. Below the slope comes the continental rise, which finally merges into the abyssal plain of the deep ocean floor.

paragraphs.heading: Where shelf sediment comes from
paragraphs.text: Passive margins, such as most Atlantic coasts, have wide, shallow shelves built of thick wedges of sediment worn over a long time from the nearby continent. Active margins have narrow, fairly steep shelves, because frequent earthquakes shift sediment into the deep sea. Shelf sediment is terrigenous, meaning it was eroded from the continents. Yet little of it comes from today's rivers: some 60–70% is relict sediment, dropped during the last ice age when the sea was 100–120 m lower.

paragraphs.heading: Sorted by distance
paragraphs.text: Sediment usually gets finer the farther it lies from the coast. Sand stays in shallow water churned by waves, while silt and clay settle in calm, deep water well offshore. These deposits pile up 15–40 centimetres every thousand years, much faster than sediment in the open deep sea.

paragraphs.heading: Rich shelf seas
paragraphs.text: The water on a shelf is pushed around by tides, by wind and by brackish water from rivers. Shallow depths and faster currents stir it up, which can make these seas very rich in life. Shelf seas cover only about 8% of the ocean's surface, yet they support 15–20% of the world's primary productivity.

paragraphs.heading: Mixed water and layered water
paragraphs.text: In temperate shelf seas, three distinct regimes arise from the tug of war between surface heating, river inflow and stirring by tides and wind. Where the water is shallow, tides are strong and rivers are far away, tidal churning beats surface heating, so the water stays mixed all year. In deeper water, summer heating wins and lays a warm surface layer over cut-off deep water. Lasting boundaries called tidal mixing fronts divide these two regimes.
